lead: A rotary inductive device turns shaft angle into an AC voltage. One winding sits on the stator, one on the rotor, and the mutual inductance between them changes as the shaft turns, so the induced voltage carries the angle in its amplitude and phase. Three devices use this idea: the induction potentiometer, the synchro pair and the microsyn. Only the microsyn is truly brushless, because its rotor carries no winding. The other two reach their rotor winding through slip rings. Their gain over a resistive potentiometer is no sliding contact and no wiper noise. Uses: radar antenna pointing, valve position feedback, AC servo error detection.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for mutual inductance and Chapter 3.2 for amplitude-plus-phase output.

sections.h3: The common idea: angle sets the coupling

blocks.text: Most of these devices put one winding on the stator and one on the rotor that follows the shaft. The excitation drives one winding; its flux crosses the air gap and links the other. The strength of that link is the mutual inductance M, in henry (H). Turning the shaft changes M smoothly: M = M<sub>max</sub> cos θ, where M<sub>max</sub> is the peak mutual inductance and θ is the shaft angle measured from maximum coupling.

By Faraday's law the output is an AC voltage at the excitation frequency f, with amplitude proportional to M and therefore to cos θ. When θ passes the null, M changes sign and the output flips 180° in phase. Amplitude gives the size of the angle, phase gives the side of the null.
The output is a carrier: a fixed-frequency AC wave whose envelope follows the shaft. A phase-sensitive demodulator turns it into a signed DC voltage. Keep f well above the fastest shaft motion.

An induction potentiometer is a rotary transformer with a distributed winding. The stator winding is spread over many slots, so its mutual inductance to the rotor winding varies smoothly with angle instead of in steps. The rotor carries a single winding, fed through slip rings, and the output is taken from the stator. Nothing slides on a resistance track.

blocks.where: e<sub>o</sub> is the output rms voltage (V); k is the coupling constant, less than 1; E<sub>x</sub> is the rms excitation voltage (V); θ is the shaft angle from electrical zero.

blocks.text: Here θ is measured from electrical zero, the position of minimum coupling, so the cos becomes a sin. The sine is linear only near the null, where sin θ ≈ θ with θ in radians. A few tens of degrees is the usual working range; beyond that the scale factor falls away. Full 360° measurement needs a resolver or a two-speed arrangement.

At the null the output is not exactly zero. Winding imperfections and space harmonics leave a residual called the null voltage, typically a few millivolts, and it sets the smallest angle the device can resolve. Against a resistive potentiometer: no sliding contact, no wear, no contact noise, but you need AC excitation and demodulation, and the range is limited. Typical uses are valve stem position and slow remote angle indication.

A synchro transmitter has a single-phase rotor on the shaft and a three-phase stator: three identical windings spaced 120° electrical. The rotor is excited. Each stator phase is coupled to the rotor axis at its own angle, so the three phase voltages are K·E<sub>r</sub>·cos θ, K·E<sub>r</sub>·cos(θ − 120°) and K·E<sub>r</sub>·cos(θ + 120°), where E<sub>r</sub> is the rotor excitation (V rms), θ is the rotor angle and K is a constant. The three voltages together fix θ over the full 360°. All three are in time phase (or antiphase) with the rotor excitation; only their amplitudes depend on θ, so despite the name this is not a three-phase supply.

The control transformer looks the same but works in reverse. Its three-phase stator is wired to the transmitter's stator, so it receives the same flux pattern; its single-phase rotor is the output. With zero set at θ<sub>R</sub> = θ<sub>T</sub>, the rotor voltage is e = E<sub>max</sub>·sin Δθ, where E<sub>max</sub> is the output at 90° error (V rms), θ<sub>R</sub> is the control transformer rotor angle and θ<sub>T</sub> is the transmitter rotor angle.

Near the null sin Δθ ≈ Δθ in radians, so the output measures the error directly, and its phase against the excitation says which way the error lies. Feed it to a servo amplifier and the motor turns until Δθ = 0. This is the standard error detector of an AC position servo, used in radar antenna pointing and valve positioners.

The two units are not interchangeable. The transmitter rotor is a low-impedance primary that must hold flux constant; the control transformer rotor is a high-impedance secondary built to give a small, clean null.

A microsyn is a compact, very sensitive angle pick-off. Its stator has four poles, each carrying a primary and a secondary coil; its rotor is a soft-iron piece shaped like a dumbbell, with no winding. The primaries are in series and set up flux through the rotor. The secondaries are connected so that, with the rotor centred over the poles, the voltages of poles 1 and 3 cancel those of poles 2 and 4. Turning the rotor lowers the reluctance under one pair and raises it under the other, so the output grows in proportion to the angle, with phase giving the direction, over a few degrees. With no rotor winding there are no slip rings, the null voltage is very small and the reaction torque is tiny, which is why microsyns are used as gyroscope and accelerometer pick-offs.

blocks.text: All three devices share the same practical checks: linearity near the null, size of the null voltage, excitation frequency and phase. A low-resistance load pulls the flux down and shifts both the scale factor and the null.

figure.caption: Worked example 1. The transmitter rotor at 30° puts 5.90 V, 0 V and 5.90 V (antiphase) on the three stator coils; the control transformer stator recreates that field, and its rotor, 10° away at 40°, gives e = 10 sin 10° = 1.74 V rms, the error that drives the servo back to zero.

spec.aria: Two circles: a synchro transmitter with its rotor at 30 degrees and a control transformer with its rotor at 40 degrees, joined by three stator wires carrying 5.90 volts, 0 volts and 5.90 volts in antiphase; the control transformer rotor gives an error of 1.74 volts rms.

traps: Using degrees in E<sub>max</sub>·Δθ. The sine form accepts degrees, but the linear form needs radians.
Assuming the control transformer output is proportional to Δθ itself. At 10° the sine is 0.174, not 0.10.
Confusing the induction potentiometer (one output winding, cannot separate θ from 180° − θ) with the synchro transmitter (three stator voltages fix the angle over 360°).

quiz.q: How are the windings of a synchro transmitter arranged?
quiz.a: A single-phase rotor on the shaft, excited from an AC supply, and a three-phase stator whose three identical windings are spaced 120° electrical apart.

quiz.q: Why does the output phase, not just the amplitude, carry information in a rotary inductive device?
quiz.a: The induced voltage is e = −jωMi, so its amplitude follows M and its sign follows the sign of M. When the shaft crosses the null, M reverses and the output flips 180°. Amplitude gives the size of the angle, phase gives the side.

quiz.q: A control transformer gives 10 V rms at 90° error. Find its output at an error of 4°.
quiz.a: e = E<sub>max</sub>·sin Δθ = 10 × sin 4° = 10 × 0.06976 = 0.698 V rms, about 0.70 V rms. The small-angle check, 10 × 0.0698 rad, agrees.

quiz.q: Why is a control transformer used only near the null, and not over a wide angle?
quiz.a: The output is E<sub>max</sub>·sin Δθ. At 30° error the sine is 0.500 while Δθ in radians is 0.524, an error of about 5%, and the gap grows with angle. At 90° the output peaks, and beyond 90° it falls although the error is larger, so the magnitude becomes ambiguous and only the phase still tells the direction.

quiz.q: Why does a microsyn not need slip rings?
quiz.a: Its rotor is a passive toothed iron piece with no winding, so no connection has to reach the rotating part. Rotation changes the tooth alignment and hence the coupling of the stator windings, which are all fixed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Resolvers, with two stator windings at 90°, and synchro-to-digital converter chips have largely replaced synchro chains; optical encoders replace both where digital position is wanted.

examples.question: A synchro transmitter (26 V rms rotor excitation, 6.81 V rms maximum per stator coil) has its rotor at θ<sub>T</sub> = 30°. Find the three stator coil voltages. The control transformer rotor is at θ<sub>R</sub> = 40° and gives 10 V rms at 90° error. Find the error angle and its output, and the way the servo should turn.
steps: Check: 5.90 + 0 − 5.90 = 0, as it must for three coils at 120°. The pattern (+, 0, −) is unique to 30° within 360°.
Control transformer output: e = E<sub>max</sub>·sin Δθ = 10 × sin 10° = 10 × 0.17365 = 1.736 V rms.
Linear check: Δθ = 10° = 0.1745 rad, E<sub>max</sub>·Δθ = 1.745 V; the two agree within 0.5 %.
The phase of e tells the sign of Δθ; the servo drives the load and the control transformer rotor from 40° back towards 30° until e = 0.
examples.answer: Stator coils 5.90 V, 0 V and 5.90 V in antiphase; Δθ = 10°, e = 1.74 V rms; the servo turns the rotor back from 40° to 30°.

examples.question: An induction potentiometer has E<sub>x</sub> = 10 V rms and k = 0.5. Find the output at 10° and 30°, the error of the linear law k·E<sub>x</sub>·θ at each, and the smallest angle it can resolve if the null voltage is 5 mV.
steps: Formula: e<sub>o</sub> = k·E<sub>x</sub>·sin θ = 5 sin θ volts.
So the device is linear to 0.5 % over ±10° but not over ±30°.
Null voltage 5 mV: the smallest readable angle is where 5 sin θ = 0.005, θ = 0.001 rad = 0.057°.
examples.answer: 0.868 V at 10° and 2.500 V at 30°; the linear law is 0.5 % and 4.7 % high; resolution about 0.06° with a 5 mV null.
